newsitem.title: GHANA: Gold Fields Ghana gets Tarkwa go-ahead.
newsitem.headline: Gold Fields Ghana gets Tarkwa go-ahead.

text.p: Ghana's Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has finally given Gold Fields Ghana Ltd the go-ahead for an open-cast gold-mining project in Tarkwa, southwest Ghana, the company's operations manager Ian Crowe said.
"Two weeks ago our environmental action plan was approved by EPA," Crowe told Reuters in an interview on Monday.

"The heap leach site is being developed, as well as the primary crusher site and basic infrastructure such as offices and the workshop. The mining contractor is about to start working on the haul road," he said.
"We are still planning to start pre-stripping on June 1 and if the rains do not cause delays we will indeed pour our first gold by the end of the year."

In its first phase the mine will produce 120,000 to 130,000 ounces of gold a year. The plan is to build up ore production and heap leach processing progressively to eight million short tons per year with an annual production of 230,000 ounces by 2000.
Proven reserves are 324 million tons of ore at 0.04 ounces per ton (almost 13 million ounces of gold), the second biggest resource in Ghana. The lifespan of the mine is about 25 years.
Expected capital cost is $125 million and the average cash cost over the first five years is expected to be $210 per ounce.
EPA approval of Gold Fields' project came months later than expected due to social aspects of the mining project, according to an EPA official.
The mining company has to move about 20,000 people living on the site.
Last year there were several demonstrations, including limited violence, in Tarkwa.

"Yes, the delay was largely because of social issues. But these have all been resolved in the past three months. We have signed another agreement with the resettlers and the EPA approved," mine manager Glyn Lewis told Reuters over the phone from Tarkwa on Wednesday.
About half of the 20,000 people to be relocated are "resettlers" who have agreed to move to new a village to be built by the company.

Most of the rest chose to be bought out and most left the area last year. A small group of about 100 of these "cash and move" villagers are holding out in their 90 percent bulldozered village, hoping to get more money, according to Lewis.

Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd holds 70 percent of Gold Fields Ghana. Other shareholders are Golden Knight Resources Inc with 17.5 percent, the government of Ghana with 10 percent and Ghana's government-controlled Social Security and National Investment Trust with 2.5 percent.
